title: Stacking-dependent anisotropic altermagnetism in V$_{1/3}$NbS$_2$
authors: Chris J. Lygouras, Nathan Prouse, Jack H. Drouin, Youzhe Chen, Laura Garcia-Gassull, Zili Feng, Mingxuan Fu, Lü Fang, Alexander I. Kolesnikov, Christina Hoffman, Yiqing Hao, Huibo Cao, Maxime A. Siegler, Robert J. Birgeneau, Roser Valentí, Satoru Nakatsuji, Collin L. Broholm
abstract: We report profound impacts of the stacking sequence of triangular lattices of magnetic transition metal ions intercalated between the layers of the van der Waals material NbS$_2$. Using single crystal x-ray and neutron diffraction, and transport and magnetization measurements, we show there are two distinct polytypes of $\rm V_{1/3}NbS_2$ with disparate easy axes of magnetization and different anomalous Hall responses. Self-consistent analysis of inelastic neutron scattering data provides evidence for oscillatory RKKY interactions that extend to 1 nm and stabilize quasi-collinear A-type altermagnetic orders in both polytypes though with perpendicular easy axes. The detailed stacking sequence of a bulk polytype crystal dramatically impact its macroscopic anomalous Hall response and magnetism, which suggests a new path to engineer the bulk properties of a layered three dimensional solid.
summary: This work reveals that the stacking sequence in $	ext{V}_{1/3}	ext{NbS}_2$ fundamentally dictates its magnetic ground state and anomalous Hall response. By combining advanced diffraction, transport measurements, and theoretical modeling of RKKY interactions, the authors demonstrate a pathway to engineer bulk properties in layered quantum magnets.
main_problem: The study investigates how the stacking sequence of magnetic ions ($	ext{V}^{3+}$) in $	ext{V}_{1/3}	ext{NbS}_2$ dictates its macroscopic magnetic properties, specifically focusing on anisotropic altermagnetism.
main_result: Two distinct polytypes (AB and ABC) exist, leading to different easy axes of magnetization and anomalous Hall responses. The stacking sequence dramatically controls the bulk magnetism by stabilizing quasi-collinear A-type antiferromagnetic order.
method: The research combines single crystal diffraction (X-ray/neutron), transport measurements (Anomalous Hall Effect), inelastic neutron scattering, and theoretical modeling using RKKY interactions and Mean-Field Theory.
model_or_system: The system is the layered van der Waals material $	ext{V}_{1/3}	ext{NbS}_2$, which forms a superlattice structure. The magnetism is modeled by Heisenberg Hamiltonians incorporating exchange couplings ($J_{ij}$) and single-ion anisotropy terms.
key_observables: Anomalous Hall resistivity ($\Deltaho_{xy}$), magnetization ($M$), spin wave excitations (INS spectra), and the magnetic ordering temperature ($T_N$).
important_parameters: The stacking sequence (AB vs. ABC) is critical; RKKY interactions extend up to 1 nm, and the system exhibits distinct transition temperatures ($\approx 50	ext{ K}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that magnetic properties are highly sensitive to structural details like stacking order, allowing for engineering of bulk electronic states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate diffraction evidence distinguishing polytypes and magnetic transitions; INS data probes spin wave dispersions across different stacking arrangements (AB vs. ABC).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from experimental characterization using diffraction and transport measurements to detailed theoretical modeling of the exchange interactions via RKKY fitting, culminating in a quantitative link between structural disorder/stacking and the resulting anomalous Hall effect.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the concept of engineering bulk properties through precise control over interlayer coupling (analogous to controlling quantum interfaces) is relevant for designing novel correlated electronic materials.
